claims.text: Configurational entropy favors a disordered, single-phase solid solution in equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles.
Differences in metal-metal bonding and atomic-size mismatch create enthalpic driving forces for local ordering or phase separation.
Competition between configurational entropy and enthalpic driving forces governs structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K.
Large local lattice distortions and short-range interactions relative to entropy stabilization increase susceptibility to ordering or elemental segregation.
Ordering or elemental segregation alters catalytic and thermoelectric properties relative to the initial state.
A slight deviation from equiatomic composition accentuates variations in local interaction energies.
At temperatures near 473 K, configurational entropy dominates and stabilizes the solid-solution structure.
Enhanced atomic mobility allows differences in bond strength and lattice strain between metals to produce ordering or phase separation.
High configurational entropy provides kinetic trapping that can be overcome by local interactions.
Ordering and phase separation change the catalytic active-site population.
Ordering and phase separation change phonon-scattering mechanisms relevant to thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles remain single-phase and preserve baseline catalytic and thermoelectric characteristics when entropy dominates or diffusion is kinetically limited.
Sufficiently long annealing produces detectable local ordering or phase separation.
A slight compositional deviation increases the enthalpic driving force for ordering or phase separation.
Detectable local ordering or phase separation correlates with a measurable decline or alteration in catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Oxidation or other extrinsic reactions can invalidate the proposed stability mechanism.
Substantially different particle sizes can cause surface effects to dominate stability.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says configurational entropy dominates near the low-temperature limit, although the thermodynamic stabilizing contribution of configurational entropy is TΔS and therefore normally becomes stronger, not weaker, as temperature rises. The text partly substitutes increasing kinetic mobility at high temperature for a reversal of the entropy-enthalpy balance.

Configurational entropy is described both as a thermodynamic stabilizer and as providing 'kinetic trapping.' Entropic stabilization and diffusion-limited kinetic trapping are distinct effects, so the stated mediator does not consistently distinguish thermodynamic stability from persistence of a metastable phase.
